stories.title: Pedestrian killed following hit-and-run in Co Kerry
stories.summary: A pedestrian has been killed after he was struck by a van in a hit-and-run in Listowel, Co Kerry. The incident happened on the N69 near Dromin Upper after 3am. The pedestrian, who was male, was pronounced dead at the scene. The N69 between Cahirdown Roundabout in Listowel and Derry in Listowel has been closed for an examination with local diversions in place. An appeal for witnesses has been issued and anyone who was travelling on N69 near Dromin Upper in Listowel between 2.30am and 4am and who may have camera footage, including dash-cam, are asked to make it available to gardaí. Anyone with information is asked to contact Listowel Garda Station on 068-50820, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111 or any garda station.

stories.title: Single homeless adults 'overlooked', warns charity
stories.summary: Simon Communities of Ireland has warned that single adults have been largely overlooked in housing policy and homelessness responses, despite being the dominant demographic living in emergency accommodation. The most recent figures from the Department of Housing show 61% of all adults living in emergency accommodation are classed as "single". This figure includes childless couples, but very many adults are experiencing homelessness on their own. "We simply won't end homelessness if we are not talking about this cohort and putting targeted resources behind it," said Ber Grogan, Executive Director of Simon Communities of Ireland. As well as representing 61% of all adults in emergency accommodation, single adult homelessness has increased by 61% in the last five years, climbing from 4,501 in July 2021 to 7,244 in July 2026. Tackling this is the focus of Simon Communities of Ireland's first national fundraising campaign: Homeless & Alone: One Big Push.

stories.title: Govt to give excise cut 'certainty for winter' - Harris
stories.summary: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris has said the Government will provide certainty around excise cuts on petrol and diesel for the winter. The Government is poised to extend the cuts until late February or early March in next month's Budget. The reductions, which were first introduced in April, were set to be unwound from the beginning of November. Speaking in the Dáil during Leaders' Questions, Mr Harris said: "Certainty for the winter period on excise is something that we can do and something that we will do." Mr Harris also pointed towards a potential cut on the carbon tax on home heating oil. He told the Dáil how he was "looking at the issue of carbon taxation in terms of how it applies to certain products" and that he was "particularly concerned around the home heating situation and the gas situation".

stories.title: CCPC searches solar panel firms over possible bid-rigging
stories.summary: A number of so-called dawn raids have been carried out by the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) of businesses active in the solar panel industry. CCPC officers, together with garda detective units and local gardaí, carried out the unannounced searches - which are part of an investigation into suspected bid-rigging in relation to public tenders. The consumer watchdog has the power to carry out such searches for information and evidence where it has reason to suspect that companies or individuals are not compliant with competition law. According to the CCPC, bid-rigging is a serious form of cartel conduct that occurs when businesses agree in advance how they will respond to a tender process, rather than competing independently. Such conduct may include agreeing who will win a contract, submitting cover bids, taking turns winning contracts, or agreeing not to bid. Such activity can lead to higher prices and poorer value for purchasers.

stories.title: Turkey and Pakistan discuss defence for Saudi Arabia
stories.summary: Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani military chiefs are to discuss help for Saudi Arabia as it faces attacks by Yemen's Houthis, while Iraq further curtailed Iranian flights ⁠in line with US pressure, and an Iranian official threatened retaliation. The Houthis have launched strikes on the Saudi-backed government in Yemen and repeatedly fired into Saudi Arabia, disrupting oil flows from the world's largest energy exporter, as part of a wider Middle East war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February. The military escalation continued this week despite a push during the UN General Assembly in New York to revive diplomacy to end the conflict, which quickly spread to Lebanon and the Gulf in March before escalating in Yemen in recent weeks. With talks stalled and during a lull in direct fire by the US and Iran, Washington had shifted tactics to extend the reach of its financial sanctions by targeting companies from third countries that do business with Iranian firms through "secondary sanctions". Iranian airlines were barred from neighbouring countries including the United Arab Emirates and Oman on Thursday in response to new US sanctions, the first big impact of the shift. The three other Iraqi airports that operate flights to and from Iran joined Baghdad airport in suspending them, sources and state media said.

stories.title: Sarsfields ready to earn their stripes as title hunters
stories.summary: Last winter was an unusual one in the East Galway parishes of New Inn and Bullaun, when for the first time in seven years, the local camogie team had no involvement in the AIB All-Ireland club series. The locals were so accustomed to following their camogie stars to different parts of the country during the winter months and inevitably arriving in Croke Park on club camogie's biggest day, that the absence of those occasions was an outlier. Such has been the success of Sarsfields camogie club since winning their first county senior title in 2016, that appearing in national finals has become the norm. Four All-Ireland and eight county championships in a glorious ten-year period has seen Sarsfields claim their place in the history books as one of camogie’s greatest ever club sides. stories.title: Knight: Israel game shouldn't be going ahead
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland midfielder Jason Knight does not believe the game against Israel on Sunday should go ahead. The Nations League meeting will take place in the Hungarian city of Debrecen, with Ireland's designated home fixture taking place in Backa Topola in Serbia on Sunday week. Manager Heimir Hallgrimsson said last week that many of his squad were uncomfortable about taking part in the game, adding: "We're not playing with genocide, we’re playing against genocide." Those comments drew a furious response from the Israel Football Association, which accused Hallgrimsson of "hypocrisy and stupidity". Speaking in the wake of last night's defeat in Pristina, Knight said: "Look, it’s difficult. "I don’t think the game obviously should be going ahead but it is going ahead. We’ll have a deeper talk about it and what that means, we’ll get our thoughts as a group and go from there.

stories.title: Wafer out as Ireland make six changes for Japan Test
stories.summary: Ireland head coach Scott Bemand has made six changes to his side to face Japan on Sunday (12.45pm) in Galway's Dexcom Stadium, with Aoife Wafer missing out due to injury. There is also a debut cap in the offing for Munster's Beth Buttimer from the bench as part of a rotated Irish selection. Cliodhna Moloney-MacDonald misses out so Neve Jones starts at hooker with Eilís Cahill making her first start at tighthead prop. The shift means that Linda Djougang will not start a Test for Ireland for just the second time since Scott Bemand took charge. Niamh O'Dowd completes the front row while Dorothy Wall and Fiona Tuite-O'Sullivan are retained in the engine room. Sale Sharks star Brittany Hogan is the other change in the pack, as she starts at blindside flanker in place of Wafer. Captain Erin King is at openside with debutant from last weekend, Connacht's Jemima Adams Verling, shifting to number eight. At half-back there is a return for Connacht's Aoibheann Reilly who makes her first start since the Rugby World Cup quarter-final defeat to France a year ago. She is partnered by Dannah O'Brien.

stories.title: Reviewed: Louise Kennedy's Stations is one of the year's best
stories.summary: There's a lot to be said for writers and artists who perfect a particular kind of narrative. Those who recognise that not every piece of storytelling has to be some convoluted exercise in experimentation or postmodern trickery. Hilary Mantel, for example, will be remembered for the way she evoked some of the most pivotal moments in European history. Seamus Heaney will be remembered for the dignity and complexity with which he imbued Irish rural life. Sally Rooney will be remembered for her scalpel-like dissections of post-Celtic Tiger Irish society. And Louise Kennedy, I dare say, will be remembered for her stories about lovers who are bound to one another, in spite – and sometimes because – of their irreconcilable differences. If the unfurling of the relationship at the centre of Kennedy’s new novel Stations feels familiar, then, it’s only because we are in the company of a writer who is at her most comfortable when she is pulling apart the meaty chambers of the human heart. The story follows Róisín McCaffrey and Red Camelin as they grow together, drift apart, reconcile and finally lose touch over the course of almost 30 years. "After he left she remembered the schoolbook Mags had taken in, I love Red Camelin printed inside the cover. IF ** KI NG LO VE RE DC AM EL IN she spelled as she fell asleep." Kennedy’s protagonists shine here – feel real – precisely because she resists any temptation to simplify or make them palatable. With all their messy quirks and foibles intact, they read more like the vivid character studies one would expect to find in a Gay Talese profile than fictional constructs from a story about 1980s Ireland. Red is introduced as the rebellious, troubled, brilliant eldest son of an outwardly conservative (and likely abusive) family dynamic. Róisín begins the novel as a refugee of sorts; one whose father was forced to move their family south to escape the danger he encountered as a Catholic member of the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC).

The Edge described being back at the school five decades later as "extraordinary" and "very moving". "I think we were good," he joked. "I think the sound was better this time, is my sense, and I was more in tune. So I was very happy.

stories.title: Things to do in Dublin this weekend (September 25-27)
stories.summary: From pop-up fashion on Grafton Street to sensory-friendly screenings in Raheny, there is plenty happening in Dublin this weekend. Woven Relations pop-up is a free event that brings an array of early-career designers together under one roof in Bewley's Grafton Street from 11am-5pm on Saturday, 26 September. Among them will be Lainey Whelan's hand-printed tights brand, T-Lainey, which has been worn onstage by award-winning singer CMAT. Attendees can purchase one-of-a-kind pieces and get to know the faces and minds behind their next favourite designers, such as Conor O’Brien Studio, Casa Cor and Moroccan brand Anouri Original. Sensinema brings a screening of The Secret of Kells to St Anne's Park, Raheny, on Saturday, 26 September 2026. Located by the Red Stable Carpark, there will be pre-screening music and chats from 3pm, with the film beginning at 4pm. Get event access guide here. Running from 24 September — 11 October, 18 days of theatre will take place all around Dublin. From world premieres and major Irish productions to extraordinary international work, some of the most exciting artists making theatre today are coming to Dublin this year. The Dublin Festival of History will run from 26 September to 11 October 2026, shining a fresh perspective on history and its importance in our everyday lives. Attracting best-selling Irish and international historians to Dublin for a high-profile programme of history talks and debate each Autumn, the festival is now celebrating its 14th year. Check out the full programme of events here. On the last Thursday of every month, Dublin stays open later. stories.title: NI court to hear challenge over Drumcree parade decision
stories.summary: A planned legal challenge to the Parades Commission of Northern Ireland's decision to allow an Orange Order parade to take place in Drumcree, Portadown will be heard at Belfast High Court at 11am. Residents from Portadown lodged a judicial review after the commission gave the Orange Order permission to march on Garvaghy Road. The body has blocked the order from marching along the road in July every year since 1998. The commission's decision allows up to 35 Orangemen to walk from Drumcree Church tomorrow morning. The commission attached conditions that the march should depart no later than 8am from Drumcree Church and disperse by 9.30am. No supporters are allowed to accompany the parade, and no bands are allowed to participate along the route.

stories.title: Europe's top junior surfers to compete in Bundoran
stories.summary: The top junior surfers from 20 countries across Europe are set to compete at the EuroSurf Junior Championships in Bundoran, Co Donegal over the next week. The ten-day championship, a stepping stone to senior international competitions, will officially open tomorrow afternoon, following a Parade of Nations in the seaside town. The championship, sanctioned by the European Surfing Federation (ESF), will see 250 surfers compete at the iconic Bundoran break known as The Peak and Tullan Strand. It is the first time that Ireland will host the biannual EuroSurf Junior Championships, having previously hosted the EuroSurf Senior Championships four times, most recently in 2011. Organised by Irish Surfing in collaboration with Saltwater Festival, the event represents a significant milestone for the sport in Ireland, ahead of the LA Olympic Games. CEO of Irish Surfing Zoe Lally, who competed in 1997 and helped organise the 2011 events in Ireland said this year's entry for the EuroSurf Juniors is the biggest on record.

stories.title: Abolishing private care in public hospitals to cost €140m
stories.summary: The HSE told the Public Accounts Committee that abolishing private practice in public hospitals will cost around €140 million this year. The HSE's Acting Chief Financial Officer Michael Lane said to understand the HSE's deficit it is important to look at "the policy change in private income". "That's a significant loss in income to us this year. Structurally, we are going to have to rebalance that and we are going to have to find a way without that income," he said. Mr Lane said it is "probably a loss of around €140 million to us this year". The committee earlier heard that the HSE incurred charges of €8.4 million for Covid vaccines in 2025 that had reached their expiry dates or were determined to no longer be clinically suitable for use, along with €1.5m for stocks of legacy and obsolete PPE. A further €6.7m was incurred by HSE in 2025 to dispose of this obsolete stock.

stories.title: Volkswagen announces global recall of almost 3m cars
stories.summary: German car giant Volkswagen has confirmed a recall of around 2.86 million vehicles worldwide over a potential steering risk, according to the German transport authority KBA. The affected models include VW's Tiguan, Touran, Golf and Caddy vehicles built between 2013 and 2024, and around 700,000 Audi models built from 2017 to 2024, the KBA said in brief statements this week. Corrosion could cause a bolt to fracture, leading to steering failure, though no such incidents have been reported, the statement said. "A corrosion problem" was discovered in quality control checks of the vehicles, a Volkswagen spokesman said. "We're now recalling the affected vehicles as a precautionary measure, and there have been no human injuries," he said, adding that drivers can continue using the vehicles until obtaining a dealer appointment for bolt replacements. Meanwhile, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume may have got the green light from stakeholders for his turnaround plan, but he faces tough talks in Germany over job cuts and plant closures as well as fundamental questions over the automaker's US strategy.

stories.title: Byrnes, Hegarty and Hayes up for Hurler of the Year
stories.summary: All-Ireland champions Limerick lead the way with 13 nominations for this year's PwC All-Stars, while the Treaty men also have two players vying for Hurler of the Year. Two former winners - Diarmaid Byrnes (2022) and Gearóid Hegarty (2020) - will go up against Cork attacker Brian Hayes for the individual award. Limerick reclaimed the Liam MacCarthy Cup this summer to complete a clean sweep, having landed the Munster and Allianz League crowns earlier in the year. Eight counties are represented in the nominations, with beaten All-Ireland finalists Galway next on the list with 11 players. Cork have seven, followed by three for fellow semi-finalists Clare, while quarter-finalists Dublin and Offaly have three and two nominations respectively. Neighbours Waterford (two) and Kilkenny (one) finish out the list. Two Galway players are going for the Young Hurler of the Year award. They are Jason Rabbitte and Cillian Trayers, with Cork's William Buckley the third player to be involved.

stories.title: Premier League joins calls for FIFA governance reform
stories.summary: The Premier League has joined forces with major European leagues in calling for a fundamental reform of FIFA, saying the organisation's governance is currently "not fit for purpose". FIFA president Gianni Infantino has faced widespread criticism and calls to quit since his plan for private investment in a commercial vehicle, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run its tournaments emerged on 28 July. Opposition from three continents forced the abandonment of the FFE plan but European football’s governing body, UEFA, insists it has nevertheless lost confidence in Infantino and says it will work to identify a credible alternative candidate to stand against him in next year’s presidential election. Infantino has this week pledged to reform FIFA, but the bosses of four of Europe’s major leagues, including the Premier League’s Richard Masters, have now co-signed a statement which said: "It is not enough for surface-level, process changes to be explored in the aftermath of FFE – fundamental governance reform is essential to restore clear constitutional boundaries within FIFA, including confidence that individual disciplinary matters remain demonstrably insulated from political interference." That last remark was a reference to the widespread discontent around FIFA’s handling of the Folarin Balogun case, with the United States striker’s one-match ban being suspended to allow him to play a World Cup last-16 match against Belgium. The suspension of the ban was enacted by FIFA’s disciplinary committee, but US President Donald Trump admitted he had personally called Infantino asking for a "review" of the ban.

stories.title: Cork school melts hearts with student-run ice cream van
stories.summary: Aaron Wolfe, Principal in Coláiste Éamann Rís in Deerpark, Co Cork, and students Alyssa and Sophia joined The Oliver Callan Show to talk about their ice cream van in Cork. Listen back above. Jumble sales and bake-offs are two old reliables when it comes to student-led businesses, but one school in Cork is certainly freezing out the competition. Coláiste Éamann Rís in Deerpark, Co Cork has launched a new student initiative: a student-run ice cream van that is already a hit with the school and locals alike. Speaking of the inspiration behind the project, Principal Aaron Wolfe says he had heard of other schools buying coffee trucks. "And I said, well we can go one better", he quips. "Kids eat ice cream, they don't drink coffee. You could put a coffee machine in an ice cream van, so rather than just being stuck with a one-sided business we have now a mobile coffee hut, we have the ice cream, we have slushies, we have everything." After a quick search online, he found an ice cream van for sale in Mayo and that was that.

stories.title: OpenAI reveals agents leaked over 50 ChatGPT user images
stories.summary: OpenAI has revealed that its agents leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users, as it continues to investigate its AI agents acting improperly. The company has declined to say if the images were AI-generated or depicted real people. It also declined to say when the images were posted. Most of the leaked images have been taken down, and OpenAI said it was lobbying hosting providers to remove the rest. OpenAI's agents had access to these images because the company relies on anonymised user data as part of its model-training process. Enterprise data is not eligible for training, while ChatGPT users must to opt out of allowing the company to use their data for training. This latest disclosure comes two months after the AI developer revealed that its models had breached Hugging Face, an open-source AI platform.

stories.title: Sport Ireland ordered to rehire sacked finance manager
stories.summary: The State body overseeing sports authorities in Ireland has been ordered to rehire a sacked finance manager to her former role after the Labour Court ruled she had been unfairly dismissed. The court heard Joanna Gurtman had been fired from her role with Sport Ireland after a report by an external investigator accused her of using her mental health to gaslight HR staff and displaying characteristics of people with "severe narcissistic disorders." However, the Labour Court upheld an appeal by Ms Gurtman against a determination by the Workplace Relations Commission that the termination of her employment contract by Sport Ireland was fair. Labour Court deputy chairperson, Niamh McGowan, said the investigation report and process was "fundamentally flawed" and not subject to any scrutiny at the disciplinary or appeal stage. Ms McGowan said it rendered the dismissal both substantively and procedurally unfair. The Labour Court said the investigation had gone beyond fact-finding to allow the investigator to decide if further action was required, while Ms Gurtman had not been provided with any evidence used by the investigator.

stories.title: EU 'ready to defend' €120m fine against Musk's X
stories.summary: The European Union has said that it was "ready to defend" its €120 million fine against Elon Musk's X platform after the United States asked a top court to let it intervene on Mr Musk's side. Mr Musk and X, formerly known as Twitter, are challenging the penalty imposed by Brussels for violating the bloc's online content rules. The US Justice Department said yesterday that it had filed an application at the EU's second-highest court backing Mr Musk and X's bid to annul the European Commission's December 2025 decision, the first fine ever issued under the Digital Services Act (DSA). "We have a very solid case that we have advanced, indeed, with a €120 million fine... and the commission is, of course, absolutely ready to defend its position in court," EU spokesman Thomas Regnier told reporters. "We have a lot of evidence at our disposal and it will be for the court to decide as always. They are fully independent," Mr Regnier added. The EU sanction against X last December followed a two-year-long investigation under the DSA, which requires online platforms to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content.

stories.title: Taiwan denounces Xi's comments to Trump in Washington
stories.summary: Taiwan's government has denounced Chinese President Xi Jinping's comments on the island's future to US President Donald Trump as a "distortion of the facts", saying only the Taiwanese people can decide their future. China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, a position President Lai Ching-te and his administration reject. Mr Xi told Mr Trump in Washington yesterday that China's position on safeguarding national "reunification" and territorial integrity is clear, and he hoped the US would adhere to the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence. Mr Xi's remarks represent "the consistent Chinese approach of distorting facts and unilaterally conveying its position and claims", Taiwan's foreign ministry said in a statement. "Taiwan's sovereignty belongs to all the people of Taiwan. The Chinese Communist Party has no right to represent the Taiwanese people, and Taiwan's future can only be determined by the Taiwanese people through democratic means," it added. The US is Taiwan's most important international backer and arms supplier despite the lack of formal diplomatic ties.

stories.title: Can Healy succeed Pogacar as cycling's elite world champ?
stories.summary: Ben Healy is hoping Tadej Pogacar’s absence from the elite World Road Race Championships in Montreal on Sunday is the key to victory. He was a superb third behind Pogacar and Remco Evenepoel in last year’s race, the best Irish result since Sean Kelly’s bronze medal in Chambery, France, in 1989. Healy has experienced a more complicated season this year but appears to be hitting peak form at precisely the right time. He’ll be up against many of the top stars of world cycling on Sunday but not Pogacar. The Slovenian crashed out on stage 8 of the Vuelta a Espana, sustaining fractures to his neck and collarbone as well as a concussion. He misses the worlds as a result. "The fact that he’s not there is pretty exciting for a lot of people. I think it’s going to make a very open, chaotic race, which is exactly what I like." Healy had his own experience of injury this year, suffering a fracture to his sacrum in the Itzulia Basque Country event. He also had a fever in the pre-Tour de France preparation race the Tour Auvergne-Rhóne-Alpes and withdrew.
